Household spending has been expanding at a moderate rate, and growth in business fixed investment has picked up in recent quarters. On a 12-month basis, both overall inflation and inflation for items other than food and energy have declined this year and are running below 2 percent. Market-based measures of inflation compensation remain low; survey-based measures of longer-term inflation expectations are little changed, on balance. Consistent with its statutory mandate, the Committee seeks to foster maximum employment and price stability. Hurricane-related disruptions and rebuilding have affected economic activity, employment, and inflation in recent months but have not materially altered the outlook for the national economy. Consequently, the Committee continues to expect that, with gradual adjustments in the stance of monetary policy, economic activity will expand at a moderate pace and labor market conditions will remain strong. Inflation on a 12âmonth basis is expected to remain somewhat below 2 percent in the near term but to stabilize around the Committee's 2 percent objective over the medium term. Near-term risks to the economic outlook appear roughly balanced, but the Committee is monitoring inflation developments closely. In view of realized and expected labor market conditions and inflation, the Committee decided to raise the target range for the federal funds rate to 1-1/4 to 1â1/2 percent. The stance of monetary policy remains accommodative, thereby supporting strong labor market conditions and a sustained return to 2 percent inflation. In determining the timing and size of future adjustments to the target range for the federal funds rate, the Committee will assess realized and expected economic conditions relative to its objectives of maximum employment and 2 percent inflation. This assessment will take into account a wide range of information, including measures of labor market conditions, indicators of inflation pressures and inflation expectations, and readings on financial and international developments. The Committee will carefully monitor actual and expected inflation developments relative to its symmetric inflation goal. The Committee expects that economic conditions will evolve in a manner that will warrant gradual increases in the federal funds rate; the federal funds rate is likely to remain, for some time, below levels that are expected to prevail in the longer run. However, the actual path of the federal funds rate will depend on the economic outlook as informed by incoming data. Voting for the FOMC monetary policy action were Janet L. Yellen, Chair; William C. Dudley, Vice Chairman; Lael Brainard; Patrick Harker; Robert S. Kaplan; Jerome H. Powell; and Randal K. Quarles. Voting against the action were Charles L. Evans and Neel Kashkari, who preferred at this meeting to maintain the existing target range for the federal funds rate.

title: Minutes of the Federal Open Market Committee
body_summary: A Federal Open Market Committee meeting was held on October 31-November 1, 2017, selecting James A. Clouse as secretary, effective November 26, 2017. The committee maintained its target range for the federal funds rate at 1-1/4 percent, considering realized and expected economic conditions. Economic activity had been rising at a solid rate, with the labor market continuing to strengthen, and above-trend economic growth was expected. Inflation on a 12-month basis was expected to remain below 2 percent in the near term but stabilize around the Committee's 2 percent objective over the medium term.

title: Federal Reserve issues FOMC statement
body_summary: Information received since the Federal Open Market Committee met in September indicates that the labor market has continued to strengthen and that economic activity has been rising at a solid rate despite hurricane-related disruptions. Household spending has been expanding at a moderate rate, and growth in business fixed investment has picked up in recent quarters. Near-term risks to the economic outlook appear roughly balanced, but the Committee is monitoring inflation developments closely. title: Minutes of the Federal Open Market Committee
body_summary: The Federal Open Market Committee held a joint meeting on September 19-20, 2017, and unanimously voted to amend its Rules Regarding Availability of Information to provide dispute resolution services for Freedom of Information Act requests. The committee maintained the federal funds rate at 1-1/4 percent due to an unchanged economic outlook. Total consumer price inflation continued to run below 2% in July, with a moderate pace expected before hurricanes Harvey and Irma. Nonfarm payroll employment rose solidly in July and August, while total industrial production declined sharply in August due to hurricane effects. Treasury yields declined, and the dollar depreciated due to investors' interpretations of FOMC communications and market perceptions of reduced U.S. fiscal policy changes. The FOMC's assessment of below-expectations inflation data and guidance on balance sheet normalization contributed to market expectations. Subprime auto loan balances decreased due to tighter lending standards, and real GDP growth was expected to continue at a solid pace with some short-term disruptions from hurricanes. PCE price inflation was estimated around 1-1/2%, below the Committee's objective.

title: Minutes of the Federal Open Market Committee
body_summary: The Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) held meetings with the Board of Governors on July 25-26, 2017. They selected Mark E. Van Der Weide as general counsel. The labor force participation rate increased in June, but private-sector job openings decreased. Average hourly earnings rose 2-1/2% over the past year. Total industrial production was flat, with mining and utilities increasing offsetting manufacturing's decline. Real personal consumption expenditures (PCE) rebounded in the second quarter driven by energy services and goods spending. The FOMC maintained the target range for the federal funds rate at 1-1/4 percent to promote maximum employment and 2% inflation.

body_summary: The Federal Open Market Committee held joint meetings with the Board of Governors on June 13-14, 2017. The committee selected Mark L.J. title: Minutes of the Federal Open Market Committee
body_summary: Janet L. Yellen, Chair of the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC), led a joint meeting with the Board of Governors on May 2-3, 2017. The Committee discussed economic conditions and monetary policy, citing improved household balance sheets, buoyant consumer sentiment, and moderate growth in residential investment and business fixed investment. Labor market conditions strengthened, with an unemployment rate of 4.5%. Inflation remained close to the FOMC's 2% target, but some participants expressed concern about progress slowing. The Committee left the federal funds rate unchanged at 3/4 to 1 percent, citing uncertainty about fiscal policy changes and awaiting additional evidence indicating that recent economic slowdown was transitory before making further adjustments.

title: Federal Reserve issues FOMC statement
body_summary: Information received since the Federal Open Market Committee met in March indicates that the labor market has continued to strengthen even as growth in economic activity slowed. Job gains were solid, on average, in recent months, and the unemployment rate declined. Household spending rose only modestly, but the fundamentals underpinning the continued growth of consumption remained solid. Business fixed investment firmed. Inflation measured on a 12-month basis recently has been running close to the Committee's 2 percent longer-run objective. Excluding energy and food, consumer prices declined in March and inflation continued to run somewhat below 2 percent. Market-based measures of inflation compensation remain low; survey-based measures of longer-term inflation expectations are little changed, on balance. Consistent with its statutory mandate, the Committee seeks to foster maximum employment and price stability. The Committee views the slowing in growth during the first quarter as likely to be transitory and continues to expect that, with gradual adjustments in the stance of monetary policy, economic activity will expand at a moderate pace, labor market conditions will strengthen somewhat further, and inflation will stabilize around 2 percent over the medium term. Near-term risks to the economic outlook appear roughly balanced. The Committee continues to closely monitor inflation indicators and global economic and financial developments. In view of realized and expected labor market conditions and inflation, the Committee decided to maintain the target range for the federal funds rate at 3/4 to 1 percent. The stance of monetary policy remains accommodative, thereby supporting some further strengthening in labor market conditions and a sustained return to 2 percent inflation. In determining the timing and size of future adjustments to the target range for the federal funds rate, the Committee will assess realized and expected economic conditions relative to its objectives of maximum employment and 2 percent inflation. This assessment will take into account a wide range of information, including measures of labor market conditions, indicators of inflation pressures and inflation expectations, and readings on financial and international developments. The Committee will carefully monitor actual and expected inflation developments relative to its symmetric inflation goal. The Committee expects that economic conditions will evolve in a manner that will warrant gradual increases in the federal funds rate; the federal funds rate is likely to remain, for some time, below levels that are expected to prevail in the longer run. However, the actual path of the federal funds rate will depend on the economic outlook as informed by incoming data. The Committee is maintaining its existing policy of reinvesting principal payments from its holdings of agency debt and agency mortgage-backed securities in agency mortgage-backed securities and of rolling over maturing Treasury securities at auction, and it anticipates doing so until normalization of the level of the federal funds rate is well under way. This policy, by keeping the Committee's holdings of longer-term securities at sizable levels, should help maintain accommodative financial conditions. Voting for the FOMC monetary policy action were: Janet L. Yellen, Chair; William C. Dudley, Vice Chairman; Lael Brainard; Charles L. Evans; Stanley Fischer; Patrick Harker; Robert S. Kaplan; Neel Kashkari; and Jerome H. Powell.

title: Minutes of the Federal Open Market Committee
body_summary: The Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) held a joint meeting with the Board of Governors on March 14-15, 2017. The committee reviewed financial markets and open market operations, reporting elevated uncertainty about U.S. economic policies and asset prices, but declining implied volatility. It affirmed its approach to balance sheet normalization, reducing securities holdings gradually and predictably, primarily by phasing out reinvestments. The Committee will reassess economic conditions before changing reinvestment policy. Total real government purchases appeared to be moving sideways in the first quarter, while consumer prices rose 2-3/4 percent over the 12 months ending in February. Foreign real GDP growth slowed slightly, but continued at a moderate pace. The FOMC meeting discussed economic projections and conditions, projecting real GDP growth to slow down before moving up, with inflation increasing gradually over the next couple of years. Participants agreed that labor market strengthening and economic activity expanding at a moderate pace posed no significant risks to inflation or stability.

title: Minutes of the Federal Open Market Committee
body_summary: Federal Reserve's Federal Open Market Committee held a joint meeting on January 31-February 1, 2017, where Chair Janet L. Yellen and other members were elected or re-elected. The Committee reaffirmed authorizations for domestic and foreign currency operations and selected Simon Potter and Lorie K. Logan to manage the System Open Market Account. It also authorized the Selected Bank to conduct standalone spot or forward transactions, warehousing, reciprocal currency arrangements, standing dollar and foreign currency liquidity swaps, and other operations in foreign currencies, subject to certain conditions and consultations with relevant authorities. The Committee reaffirmed its FOREIGN CURRENCY DIRECTIVE, authorizing the Selected Bank to execute open market transactions and maintain reciprocal currency arrangements with foreign central banks. The meeting also discussed accommodative financing conditions, improved investor sentiment, and positive economic news, including a strengthening labor market, increased business investment, and stable financial conditions. The Committee expected gradual interest rate increases due to rising inflation expectations, but some participants cautioned against adjusting monetary policy based on uncertain fiscal policies.
